title: Propexo CEO Featured in Article "The Future of the Property Management System"
summary: Remen shares his thoughts on why proptech integrations are challenging relative to other industries
body_text: Remen Okoruwa, Co-founder and CEO of Propexo, was recently featured in an in-depth analysis exploring the evolution and future of property management systems (PMS). Drawing from his experience as a former HubSpot Senior PM, Okoruwa highlighted the stark contrast between traditional software platforms and current PMS solutions, noting that proptech companies spend significant engineering resources on PMS integration maintenance. In the article, Okoruwa advocated for a more open, API-first approach similar to platforms like Salesforce and HubSpot, while explaining how Propexo's unified API solution helps companies efficiently connect with multiple property management systems. The feature also explored Propexo's unique position in the ecosystem, where they maintain both collaborative and arms-length relationships with PMS platforms as they work to modernize real estate technology integration. You can read the full article at Thesis Driven .

title: El Creciente Papel de la IA en México: Insights del Evento Integreat CDMX 2024
summary: El pasado 28 de mayo, asistimos al evento Integreat en la Ciudad de México, un encuentro que reunió a líderes en marketing, ventas y tecnología para explorar la integración de estrategias y tecnologías de inteligencia artificial (IA) con el fin de mantener la competitividad en Internet.
body_text: El pasado 28 de mayo, asistimos al evento Integreat en la Ciudad de México, un encuentro que reunió a líderes en marketing, ventas y tecnología para explorar la integración de estrategias y tecnologías de inteligencia artificial (IA) con el fin de mantener la competitividad en Internet. Desde Comscore, aprovechamos esta oportunidad para presentar un panorama del estado de Internet y la inteligencia artificial en México. Durante nuestra presentación, resaltamos varios hallazgos importantes sobre el uso de la IA tanto a nivel regional como global. A nivel mundial, las herramientas de inteligencia artificial están viendo un notable incremento en su adopción. Por ejemplo, OpenAI registró más de 676 millones de visitas y 141 millones de visitantes únicos solo en marzo de 2024. Enfocándonos en México, observamos un notable aumento en el interés por OpenAI. De enero a marzo de 2024, las visitas a OpenAI en México crecieron un 84%, mientras que la audiencia aumentó un 48%, alcanzando 6.2 millones de visitantes únicos en marzo. Además, analizamos los dispositivos que generan más tráfico hacia OpenAI y descubrimos que el 64% de los visitantes únicos acceden exclusivamente mediante laptops o computadoras de escritorio. Sin embargo, la aplicación móvil de ChatGPT también está ganando popularidad, alcanzando un millón de visitantes únicos. Al examinar los segmentos y afinidades de la audiencia de OpenAI, encontramos que el sitio tiene un alcance 2.77 veces mayor entre las personas de 18 a 24 años (índice de afinidad = 277) en comparación con su alcance promedio en Internet. Este dato subraya el impacto particular de la IA entre los jóvenes, quienes están adoptando estas tecnologías a un ritmo acelerado. Aunque OpenAI fue el caso de estudio principal en el evento, también se destacaron otras plataformas de IA generativa. Por ejemplo, Character.ai está redefiniendo el diseño de chatbots y avatares, mientras que Wondershare ha mejorado la edición de videos y presentaciones, mostrando la versatilidad y el potencial transformador de la IA generativa en diversas aplicaciones. La inteligencia artificial generativa ha logrado posicionarse como una herramienta clave en la creación de contenido, especialmente entre los jóvenes. Su capacidad para escribir, editar y diseñar está transformando la forma en que interactuamos con la tecnología. Con la continua evolución de esta tecnología, es probable que veamos un aumento aún mayor en su uso en los próximos años. Participar en el evento Integreat 2024 fue una experiencia enriquecedora que subrayó la importancia de la inteligencia artificial en el panorama actual y futuro. A medida que estas tecnologías continúan evolucionando, es crucial que las empresas y los profesionales se mantengan informados y adaptativos para aprovechar al máximo las oportunidades que la IA ofrece. title: Weave Raises $13.5M Series A to Build Engineering and Token Intelligence
summary: Weave combines LLMs and domain-specific machine learning to understand engineering work. We understand how much work was done by AI vs. humans. How much AI is helping your team ship faster, if it's having an impact on code quality and code reviews.
body_text: We started Weave to answer a question every engineering leader is now asking: what is our AI spend actually returning? Since then, our platform has analyzed more than 2 million human and AI code contributions across 20,000+ engineers at 1,000+ companies, including Robinhood, Reducto, and PostHog. Today, we're announcing our $13.5M Series A led by Standard Capital , with participation from Y Combinator, Moonfire, Burst Capital, IrregEx, and the Agent Fund. This funding accelerates our mission to become the operating system that measures and optimizes how engineers and AI impact business outcomes. The problem: tokenmaxxing is costing companies billions Companies are pouring tens of billions of dollars into AI coding tools, but when an AI can generate thousands of lines of code in seconds, teams inadvertently optimize for volume over real engineering progress. Legacy metrics like commit counts, lines of code, DORA, SPACE were built for human output, so they actively reward artificial bloat and create a false illusion of velocity. Everyone has always known the best engineers sometimes write negative lines of code. Now the problem is worse, because the code being counted isn't even written by people. The result is that executives are flying blind. They're paying for generated tokens instead of business value, with no way to calculate the true ROI of their AI spend. Half the money is being wasted, and nobody knows which half. Engineers are burning tokens by using the best model on every prompt. This is rarely necessary but it's the default state as it takes manual work to switch off and there's typically no incentive internally to optimize AI spend. Weave is build to fix this. Where we are today LLMs can look at code and understand what it's actually doing, so we trained our own model to do exactly that: read every pull request, review, and deployment, attribute it to human or AI contribution, and normalize it into a single, objective unit of output. Our model asks a simple question of every piece of work: how long would this have taken a human in the pre-AI era? From there, everything else follows: Code Output : a fair, normalized view of productivity by team or individual engineer, human and AI alike. AI ROI : a real dollar figure. For every dollar spent on tokens, how many hours of human-era engineering work are you getting? AI Skills : show engineers exactly where and how to get better at working with agents. Prompt Routing : use your own production data to route every query to the cheapest model that won't sacrifice quality or speed, including open source models, directly inside Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex. It looks at every turn and reclassifies what the best model for that prompt will be. The router is the beginning of the optimization layer. Because we see the entire path from prompt to production, our routing decisions get better over time: we know not just how a model answered, but how that answer performed once it shipped. Complex system design goes to a frontier model. Centering a button doesn't need one. Customers using the router have cut costs anywhere from 20 to 80 percent, and more importantly, teams adopting the full stack are seeing 20 to 25 percent increases in output for the same spend. What our customers (Robinhood, Telnyx and Posthog) have seen Robinhood came to us because their internal pipelines and default tool analytics couldn't tell them the most basic thing: how much of our code is actually written by AI, and is it helping? As a financial institution with a self-hosted deployment and serious security requirements, they needed answers without compromise. Telnyx runs about 150 engineers with a single VP of Engineering and no managers. Instead of relying on managers to coordinate and coach, every engineer sees their own data and uses it to level up. As David Casem, Co-Founder and CEO of Telnyx, put it: "Our goal is to ship the highest quality product as quickly and efficiently as possible for our customers. We use Weave to get objective measurement of our teams and agents as well as ways to optimize." Posthog let's all 80+ software engineers on their team see their own data, optimize their workflows and have some friendly competition. The headlines saying AI barely helps enterprises? We've found it's an implementation problem. Working with some of the fastest-growing engineering teams in the world, we don't see 10 percent lifts. We see 200 to 300 percent and our team of FDEs is built to unlock this for you. What comes next This funding will be focused on three priorities: Deeper models : advancing our code output and routing models so every measurement and every routing decision gets more accurate as the data compounds. The learning loop : closing the loop from measurement to optimization, so Weave doesn't just tell you what happened, it makes every engineer and every agent better. Customer success : supporting our growing enterprise deployments, including self-hosted environments with enterprise-grade security. The agent era will produce more software than any era before it. Engineers are becoming managers of agents, and a new role is emerging between engineering and finance: deciding where compute, tokens, and human attention should go. Those decisions need data. When product analytics arrived, not measuring your product became unthinkable, and entire new functions like growth were born. We believe the same is true now: not measuring your AI is like not measuring your product. Weave is the tool those teams of the future will be built on. The era of tokenmaxxing is over. Lines of code are dead as a metric. What replaces them is one objective measure of real output, human and AI, so engineering can finally be managed like every other part of the business. Thank you to everyone on this journey To our investors: thank you for believing in us. Dalton Caldwell, Paul Buchheit, and Bryan Berg at Standard Capital have been true partners from the first conversation, and we're grateful to Y Combinator, Moonfire, Burst Capital, IrregEx, and the Agent Fund for backing us early. As Dalton put it: "AI spend is the most powerful force in the world, and right now there is not an easy way to measure it. The opportunity for Weave is to enable every organization to effectively track and route their spend." To our customers: thank you for betting on a young startup. From Robinhood to Telnyx to PostHog, you trusted us with a question nobody had answered before, and you're the reason our models keep getting better. To the Weave team: you took on a problem that was previously thought impossible, actually measuring software engineering, and you solved it. Five days a week, in person, in San Francisco, pushing the cutting edge of what an engineering team can be. This is just the beginning.

title: Jennifer L. Slater as the new President and CEO of Strattec Security Corporation
summary: Jennifer L. Slater as the new President and CEO of STRATTEC SECURITY CORPORATION
body_text: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE STRATTEC SECURITY CORPORATION Names Senior Automotive Parts Executive as CEO MILWAUKEE – The Board of Directors (“Board”) of STRATTEC SECURITY CORPORATION (NASDAQ:STRT) (the “Company”) is proud to announce the appointment of Jennifer L. Slater as the Company’s President and Chief Executive Officer and Board member, each effective July 1, 2024. Slater is a senior executive at Sensata Technologies, Inc. with over 25 years of experience as a leader and a manager. Her experience includes general management, engineering, finance, sales and strategy. She has delivered results for owners across a diverse set of enterprises that include publicly traded companies, privately held firms, and private equity owners. Board Chair, F. Jack Liebau, Jr., said that “Slater is the right choice to lead the Company considering her extensive experience in the automotive industry. We are delighted to welcome Jen to STRATTEC – her past successes with critical leadership initiatives at major companies demonstrated that she is the right person for the job. Her focus on growth and increasing shareholder value is in step with the Board’s goals.” Liebau continued “We thank Rolando Guillot for his effective efforts as our interim President and Chief Executive Officer. We’re grateful for his hard work, leadership, and dedication to the shareholders, employees, and clients of STRATTEC. I’d also like to thank the Board’s search committee, led by Board member Tina Chang, for its tireless work. Jen immediately emerged as the top candidate of the committee, comprised of Tina, Tom Florsheim, Bruce Lisman, and me.” Slater is currently the Executive Vice President and General Manager, Performance Sensing, for Sensata Technologies, Inc. In the past year, she led the business through a significant transformation to an electrified product and systems business from an internal combustion business. She did that with a balanced focus on near term execution and intermediate term goals to deliver on a five year growth plan. Slater has delivered strong results and innovative solutions, as she moves from vision and strategy to execution. Slater currently serves as a director for Valvoline Inc. She previously worked as Group Vice President and General Manager Global OE for Clarios, LLC, where she was responsible for shaping all aspects of the advanced technology, product management, engineering and launch to support the growth of a $3.3 billion battery business. She worked at Johnson Controls International plc for 11 years in a series of senior positions, finishing her time there as Vice President Finance, Power Solutions. Slater said she is excited to lead the prominent automotive parts manufacturer. “I am honored and thrilled to lead this well-respected manufacturer as we all work together to position STRATTEC for continued growth in the automotive products industry. I am looking forward to leveraging my experience with the support of the talented employees of the company to continue to make an impact,” Slater continued. A graduate of the University of Michigan at Dearborn, Slater also earned her master’s degree in business administration from Walsh College. She has been active in the Milwaukee community, including being the Milwaukee lead for a volunteer program that brings science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) education to life and helps to spark the interest for elementary students into engineering professions and is looking forward to continuing to support the community. About STRATTEC STRATTEC designs, develops, manufactures and markets automotive Access Control Products, including mechanical locks and keys, electronically enhanced locks and keys, steering column and instrument panel ignition lock housings, latches, power sliding side door systems, power lift gate systems, power deck lid systems, power tailgate systems for trucks, door handles and related products. These products are provided to customers in North America, and on a global basis through a unique strategic relationship with WITTE Automotive of Velbert, Germany and ADAC Automotive of Grand Rapids, Michigan. Under this relationship, STRATTEC, WITTE and ADAC market each company’s products to global customers as cooperating partners of the “VAST Automotive Group” brand name. STRATTEC’s history in the automotive business spans 115 years. Contact: Dennis Bowe Vice President and Chief Financial Officer 414-247-3399 (###)

title: Chargeback Timeline: A Merchant's Tactical Guide to Key Deadlines
summary: Master the chargeback timeline with this tactical guide for merchants. Learn critical deadlines, card network rules, and strategies to win disputes and protect your revenue.
body_text: Chargebacks can feel like a labyrinth of deadlines and regulations, threatening your hard-earned revenue and consuming valuable resources. For merchants, understanding the intricacies of the chargeback timeline isn't just good practice—it's essential for survival. Each step in the payment dispute process is governed by strict time limits, and missing even one can result in an automatic loss, turning a recoverable transaction into lost revenue. This comprehensive guide cuts through the confusion, offering a tactical roadmap to the chargeback timeline. You'll gain clear, actionable insights into every stage, network-specific deadlines, and proactive strategies to protect your business. By empowering you with the knowledge to effectively manage disputes, this guide aims to significantly boost your recovery success and help you master the chargeback timeline. Understanding the Chargeback Timeline: A Merchant's Overview The chargeback timeline refers to the entire sequence of events and associated deadlines that govern a payment dispute, from the moment a cardholder initiates it to the final resolution. For merchants, this timeline is not merely a bureaucratic process; it is a critical framework that dictates their ability to defend transactions, recover revenue, and minimize financial losses. A deep understanding of these timeframes is paramount for any business accepting card payments. Merchants must recognize that every step in the chargeback process is time-sensitive. From receiving the initial notification to submitting compelling evidence, and potentially navigating arbitration, each action has a defined window. Adhering to these deadlines is not optional; it is the difference between winning a dispute and automatically forfeiting funds, impacting both revenue protection and operational efficiency. Why the Chargeback Timeline is Crucial for Merchants Ignoring or misunderstanding the chargeback timeline carries direct and severe financial consequences. Missing a deadline for submitting evidence, for instance, typically results in an automatic loss of the dispute, meaning the merchant loses the transaction amount, any associated fees, and potentially faces increased chargeback ratios. This directly impacts revenue protection and can lead to higher processing costs or even account termination by payment processors. Beyond the immediate financial hit, the operational burden of poorly managed chargebacks is significant. Teams spend valuable time chasing information, responding late, or dealing with unnecessary losses that could have been avoided with timely action. Strategic chargeback management relies heavily on a proactive approach to these deadlines, transforming a reactive scramble into an organized defense strategy. Key Phases of the Chargeback Journey The chargeback journey is a multi-stage dispute lifecycle, each with its own set of rules and chargeback time limits. Understanding these chargeback stages at a high level sets the foundation for diving into the specific deadlines and actions required at each point. Phase Description Key Action Required Typical Timeframe Cardholder Dispute Initiation Cardholder contacts their issuing bank to dispute a transaction Merchant receives notification and must acknowledge 60-180 days from transaction (varies by network/reason code) Chargeback Notification Issuing bank notifies acquiring bank, which then notifies merchant Merchant must indicate intent to fight or accept chargeback 7-10 days to acknowledge Representment Merchant submits compelling evidence to counter cardholder claim Compile and submit evidence package to acquiring bank 30-45 days from notification Pre-Arbitration/Pre-Compliance Issuing bank provides additional reasons for rejecting representment Merchant can submit further evidence or accept chargeback 10-20 days to respond Arbitration Card network acts as final arbiter, reviewing all evidence Merchant submits final evidence (if proceeding) 10-20 days after arbitration request (can extend for weeks/months) The Core Stages of a Chargeback Dispute and Their Timelines Navigating the chargeback process steps requires a detailed understanding of each stage and its associated chargeback dispute timeline. Each phase presents a unique challenge and opportunity for merchants to either defend their transaction or accept the loss. Proactive engagement at every step is crucial for optimizing chargeback resolution and protecting revenue. From the initial alert to the final arbitration decision, the clock is always ticking. Merchants must be prepared to act swiftly and strategically, gathering the necessary documentation and adhering to strict chargeback time limits. This section breaks down these critical stages, offering a clear roadmap for what to expect and how to respond effectively. Initial Dispute & Notification (First Chargeback) The chargeback notification marks the beginning of the formal chargeback timeline. Once a cardholder disputes a transaction with their issuing bank, that bank notifies the acquiring bank, which then informs the merchant. This notification is typically delivered via email, merchant portal, or API, and it immediately starts the clock on the merchant's response window. This initial first chargeback notification is critical because it sets the very first chargeback time limits for the merchant to acknowledge the dispute and begin compiling evidence. Merchants usually have a short window, often between 7 to 10 days, to indicate their intent to fight the chargeback. Missing this initial response window can lead to an automatic dispute loss, underscoring the urgency of prompt action and efficient internal processes. Merchant Response (Representment) Representment is the merchant's formal response to a chargeback, where they present compelling evidence to the issuing bank to refute the cardholder's claim. The representment timeline is one of the most critical phases, typically allowing merchants between 30 to 45 days from the chargeback notification date to submit their evidence package. This merchant response time varies slightly by card network and reason code. During this period, merchants must gather all relevant documentation, such as proof of delivery, transaction receipts, communications with the customer, and IP addresses. The quality and completeness of this evidence are paramount. A well-constructed representment package, submitted within the stipulated chargeback time limits, significantly increases the chances of winning the dispute and recovering the funds. Pre-Arbitration & Arbitration If a merchant's representment is unsuccessful, the issuing bank may choose to escalate the dispute. This can lead to a pre-arbitration or pre-compliance stage, depending on the card network. Here, the issuing bank provides additional information or reasons for rejecting the representment, giving the merchant a final opportunity to either accept the chargeback or submit further evidence. The chargeback arbitration timeline for this stage is typically shorter, often around 10-20 days. Should the dispute remain unresolved after pre-arbitration, it can proceed to arbitration, the final stage of the chargeback process. In arbitration, the card network (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) acts as the final arbiter, reviewing all submitted evidence from both sides to render a binding decision. Arbitration involves additional fees, making it a costly last resort. The arbitration timeline can extend for several weeks or even months, but the merchant's final opportunity to submit evidence for this stage is usually within a designated window, often 10-20 days after the arbitration request. Card Network-Specific Chargeback Timelines: What Merchants Need to Know A crucial aspect of mastering the chargeback timeline is understanding that deadlines are not universal. Each major card network—Visa, Mastercard, American Express, and Discover—operates under its own distinct set of rules and timeframes. What might be a standard chargeback time limit for one network could be entirely different for another. Merchants must therefore be intimately familiar with these network rules to avoid costly missteps. Ignoring these variations can lead to missed deadlines and automatic dispute losses. A tactical approach requires merchants to tailor their response strategies based on the specific card network involved in the dispute. This section provides a detailed breakdown of the chargeback deadlines for each major player, offering essential insights for effective chargeback management. Visa Chargeback Timelines Visa's chargeback rules are governed by its Visa Claims Resolution (VCR) system, designed to streamline the dispute process. For merchants, the VCR system often presents a representment timeline of approximately 30 days from the dispute processing date, though this can vary slightly based on the specific reason code. Visa categorizes disputes into "Fraud " and "Non-Fraud " flows, each with distinct evidence requirements and response paths. Read more about Visa reason codes in general here , or check out our blog if you're looking for guidance on a specific reason code. Under VCR, many disputes are resolved earlier through an " automation " process, but merchants still must be prepared to respond within the VCR timeline if a dispute proceeds to the " collaboration " phase. Prompt action, including providing comprehensive evidence like proof of authorization, transaction history, and customer communications, is vital for a successful defense within Visa's framework. Mastercard Chargeback Timelines Mastercard's dispute timeline also features specific windows for merchants. Generally, a merchant has about 45 days from the chargeback processing date to submit their first presentment (representment) response. If the dispute escalates, the issuing bank can initiate a " second presentment, " giving the merchant another opportunity to respond, typically within a 10-day window. The Mastercard chargeback periods are characterized by distinct stages including first presentment, second presentment, and potentially arbitration. Merchants must ensure their evidence directly addresses the chargeback reason code and is submitted within these strict Mastercard dispute timeline windows. Accurate and timely documentation, such as proof of service, account verification, and clear refund policies, are essential for navigating Mastercard's process. Read more about Mastercard reason codes in general here , or check out our blog if you're looking for guidance on a specific reason code. American Express Chargeback Timelines American Express (Amex) operates a somewhat different chargeback process compared to Visa and Mastercard, often involving a " retrieval request " stage before a full chargeback. Amex typically allows merchants 20 days to respond to a retrieval request, providing transaction details. If a chargeback follows, merchants generally have 20 days to respond to the chargeback itself, though this can vary. The Amex dispute time limits are known for being stringent, emphasizing quick and precise responses. Amex often requires specific types of evidence, such as signed sales slips or proof of service, depending on the dispute reason. Merchants dealing with Amex disputes need to be particularly vigilant about these shorter Amex chargeback timeline windows and ensure their evidence is tailored to Amex's requirements. Discover & Other Network Timelines Discover also has its own chargeback rules and timeframes, though they often align more closely with Mastercard or Visa in terms of overall structure. Merchants typically have around 30-45 days to respond to a Discover chargeback notification. Like other networks, Discover emphasizes the importance of providing clear and relevant evidence within the Discover chargeback timeline. For merchants operating globally, or accepting niche card brands, it is important to remember that other card network timelines will also exist. While major networks cover most transactions, specific regional or specialized card brands will have their own unique payment dispute deadlines. Merchants should consult their acquiring bank or payment processor for detailed information on these less common networks to ensure full compliance. Comparison Table: Key Card Network Deadlines Understanding the varying chargeback deadlines comparison across different card networks is critical for merchants. This table provides a concise overview of typical merchant response windows for initial representment, though specific reason codes or dispute flows may alter these timeframes. Always consult your acquiring bank or payment processor for the most current and precise network timelines chart. Card Network Initial Merchant Response Deadline (Representment) Pre-Arbitration/Second Presentment Window Arbitration Window Visa 30 days (from dispute processing date) 10-20 days 10-20 days Mastercard 45 days (from chargeback processing date) 10 days (Second Presentment) 10-15 days American Express 20 days (from chargeback notification date) Varies (often integrated) Varies Discover 30-45 days (from chargeback notification date) Varies (similar to Mastercard) Varies Note: These are general guidelines. Actual deadlines can vary based on specific reason codes, regional rules, and processor policies. Always confirm with your payment processor. Merchant Response Deadlines: Critical for Winning Disputes For merchants, the chargeback timeline is a race against the clock, where every merchant response deadline is a critical juncture. The ability to win a chargeback dispute hinges significantly on submitting a timely and complete response. Failing to adhere to these chargeback time limits almost invariably results in an automatic loss, regardless of the validity of the merchant's case. This section focuses on the merchant's direct responsibilities and the strategic importance of timely action. Understanding how long to respond to chargeback notifications and evidence requests is not just about compliance; it's about actively protecting revenue and maintaining a healthy chargeback ratio. Proactive management of these deadlines is a cornerstone of effective chargeback defense. Initial Notification Response Windows Upon receiving a chargeback notification, merchants enter a crucial response window that dictates their next steps. This initial window, often as short as 7 to 10 calendar days, is for acknowledging the dispute and signaling intent to fight. It's not necessarily for submitting full evidence, but rather for confirming receipt and initiating the process. This swift chargeback alert response is vital. Many payment processors offer automated systems or portals where merchants can quickly register their intent to dispute. Delaying this initial acknowledgment can cause the merchant to miss the opportunity to defend the transaction entirely, leading to an automatic forfeiture of funds and compounding the financial loss. Compelling Evidence Submission Deadlines The compelling evidence timeline is arguably the most important merchant response deadline. This is the period, typically 30 to 45 days from the chargeback notification, during which merchants must compile and submit a robust package of evidence to their acquiring bank. This evidence is then forwarded to the issuing bank to counter the cardholder's claim. Effective evidence submission requires meticulous organization and a deep understanding of what constitutes " compelling evidence " for each chargeback reason code. This includes transaction receipts, proof of delivery, customer communication logs, IP addresses, and any other data that supports the legitimacy of the transaction. Missing this deadline means the opportunity to present a defense is lost, and the chargeback will likely be upheld. Consequences of Missing a Deadline Missing a deadline in the chargeback timeline has severe and multifaceted consequences. Understanding these impacts is crucial for prioritizing timely responses. Consequence Type Immediate Impact Long-Term Impact Financial Loss Transaction amount debited, chargeback fee assessed Reduced profitability and cash flow disruption Automatic Dispute Loss No opportunity to present evidence or defense Permanent loss of disputed funds regardless of case validity Chargeback Ratio Impact Single missed deadline contributes to higher ratio Pattern of missed deadlines leads to increased processing fees Account Status Temporary impact on merchant standing Placement on MATCH list (Terminated Merchant File), potential account termination Operational Burden Time wasted on lost cause disputes Reduced efficiency, strained resources, decreased team morale Common Delays and How to Avoid Them in the Chargeback Timeline Even with a clear understanding of the chargeback timeline, merchants can encounter various obstacles that lead to chargeback delays. These delays can be as detrimental as missing a deadline outright, as they can prevent the timely submission of compelling evidence or slow down the overall chargeback resolution. Identifying and mitigating these common pitfalls is key to avoiding chargeback losses and maintaining an efficient chargeback process flow. Proactive strategies focusing on internal process optimization and clear communication can significantly reduce these delays. By streamlining workflows and ensuring all parties are aligned, merchants can navigate the complex chargeback timeline more effectively, improving their chances of successful representment and protecting their revenue. Internal Process Bottlenecks One of the most frequent causes of chargeback delays stems from internal process bottlenecks. Identifying and addressing these issues is critical for timely chargeback response. Common Bottleneck Impact on Response Time Solution Disorganized Record-Keeping Delays in finding transaction details, customer communications, and shipping information Centralize all customer and transaction data in accessible system Slow Information Retrieval Time wasted searching multiple systems or requesting information from different departments Integrate systems for rapid data access Lack of Clear Ownership Uncertainty about who should handle chargeback, leading to delays in assignment Define roles and responsibilities for chargeback response team Undefined Workflows No standard process for handling chargebacks, causing inconsistent response times Establish clear, documented workflows for chargeback management Insufficient Training Team members unsure of requirements or processes, leading to mistakes and delays Provide regular training on chargeback processes and requirements Communication Gaps with Banks Another significant source of delay in the chargeback timeline can be communication gaps with banks. Understanding and proactively managing these gaps is essential for timely response. Communication Issue Impact Prevention Strategy Delayed Notifications Reduced time available to respond Establish direct integration or automated notification systems Unclear Information Requests Confusion about what evidence is needed Proactively request clarification on ambiguous requests Slow Bank Responses Delays in receiving necessary information or confirmation Set up regular check-ins with payment processor Inconsistent Communication Channels Messages lost or delayed due to wrong channels Establish preferred methods for chargeback notification and evidence submission Lack of Bank Contact Information Difficulty reaching bank when questions arise Maintain clear contact list for chargeback-related inquiries Leveraging Technology for Optimal Chargeback Timeline Management The complexity and strict deadlines of the chargeback timeline make manual management an increasingly challenging and error-prone task for growing businesses. This is where technology, specifically chargeback management software, becomes an invaluable asset. Automated solutions can significantly streamline dispute tracking and response, ensuring merchants never miss a critical deadline and can focus on strategic defense rather than administrative burden. Integrating technology into chargeback management not only enhances efficiency but also provides a tactical advantage. Platforms like Dispute Ninja are designed to simplify the intricate process of adhering to chargeback time limits across various card networks, offering a robust solution for businesses looking to optimize their chargeback recovery and protect their revenue. Automated Alerts and Deadline Tracking Specialized chargeback management software provides critical automation that prevents missed deadlines and ensures timely responses. Feature Benefit Impact Real-Time Chargeback Notifications Immediate awareness of new disputes via direct processor integration Enables faster response initiation Automatic Deadline Calculation System calculates remaining time for each response deadline Eliminates manual tracking errors Proactive Deadline Reminders Automated notifications as deadlines approach Prevents oversight and ensures maximum preparation time Real-Time Timeline Visibility Clear view of chargeback timeline for all open disputes Enables better prioritization and resource allocation Multi-Network Deadline Tracking Handles different deadline rules for Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Discover Ensures compliance across all card networks Streamlining Evidence Submission Technology plays a pivotal role in streamlining evidence submission, automating what would otherwise be a time-consuming manual process. title: What is a context warehouse?
summary: A context warehouse is a data warehouse wired directly into the tools and agents that act on it, so no data has to move from one tool to another to be useful.
body_text: What is a context warehouse? Lizzie Epton Jul 21, 2026 Data warehouse , Infrastructure , PostHog news Contents Data warehouses are optimized for analytics, business intelligence (BI), and data engineers. What would they look like if they optimized for AI agents instead? They'd look like context warehouses: a single tool that stores your business and product data, ingests and models it, and makes it directly available to agents that want to reference and use it as context. This isn't just an agent bolted onto a data warehouse, or a smarter semantic layer sitting on top of one. Plenty of data warehouses have that. A context warehouse is different because the ingestion pipeline and the modeling that make raw data mean something are part of the same tool as the storage and the querying, not separate pieces you assemble and keep in sync yourself. Nothing has to be piped from one system to another to be useful. Here's how we're thinking about the differences between a data and context warehouse, and how we're building one at PostHog. Why "data warehouse" stopped being the right word A data warehouse's job is simple: store structured data and let you query it. It doesn't know what a "customer" is, what a feature flag is, or what an experiment variant is; someone has to teach it, by building the modeling and pipelines to wire that meaning in. Traditionally that's a data engineer's job. As agents increasingly become the consumer of data, they need both the access and the tools to make sense of this data themselves. It becomes their job to know the meaning of the data so they can decide what to fix next. An agent working the self-driving product loop needs product signals (errors, funnel drops, slow sessions) and business context (revenue, plan tier, support history) in the same place so it can query directly without waiting for your daily data sync. That's what a context warehouse is: a data warehouse plus ingestion pipeline and data modeling, with direct access to your agents in one place. It’s what you get without having to build and maintain it. Data warehouse vs. context warehouse The difference isn't the storage engine, it's what's allowed to touch the data without a pipeline standing in between. Data Warehouse Context Warehouse What data is included? Whatever you pipe in, on tables you define, including via your own batch export jobs Product events (already there, no export job to build) + data you pipe in What can query it without extra glue? Your data warehouse's query engine and AI agent Every tool built on top of it, natively. For PostHog that's Analytics, Experiments, Feature Flags, the SQL editor, PostHog AI, and MCP-connected agents Who owns it? A dedicated data team Product engineers, with or without a data team It's for you if you need… Scale and governance for structured data The full context layer your product and your agents run on Who a context warehouse is for (and who it isn't, yet) It's a good fit if: You're AI-pilled and ship an increasing amount of work through agents and loops, or you want to make your product self-driving. You haven't built a data stack yet, and want product data and business context queryable by an agent from day one instead of assembling a data engineer's worth of tooling first. You're an engineer-led team tired of maintaining ETL pipelines whose only job is keeping two systems in sync so a human (or now, an agent) can ask a question that spans both. It's not the right fit, yet, if: You run a data org with mature dbt pipelines and advanced modeling needs we don't match yet. You want a warehouse and nothing else. The integrated platform is the point, if that's not what you're looking for, a standalone warehouse might be a better fit. How our context warehouse works at PostHog Get all your data in Your context warehouse starts with data that's already there. Once enabled, PostHog mirrors your product event data to S3, partitioned by organization, as it's captured with no pipeline to build. Everything else comes in through Warehouse Sources : 200+ integrations that sync external systems including Stripe, HubSpot, Salesforce, Postgres, and more. Connecting each source is no-code and takes under two minutes, or even more hands-off with the PostHog Wizard. Compare that to an ETL pipeline: writing and maintaining extraction jobs, hosting them somewhere, wiring up a destination, and debugging it every time a schema changes upstream. Warehouse Sources allows you to skip all of that. Store your data Under the hood, we store all your data in our rebuilt Managed Warehouse . It's a DuckDB instance per organization sitting on an S3 data lake that you have full access and ownership over your data through. The main ingredients: Storage: S3, partitioned per organization. Once enabled, product events land here automatically; Warehouse Sources syncs external systems into the same bucket. Compute & isolation: A DuckDB instance per organization, running in its own Firecracker MicroVM (the same technology AWS uses for Lambda), so no query competes with anyone else's. Lifecycle: A lifecycle service sleeps instances when idle and wakes them when a query arrives, in roughly 300ms. You're billed when a worker is running, and they automatically shut down when idle after 60s. Access: A Postgres wire protocol endpoint. Connect with psql, point a BI tool at it, or wire it into an agent over MCP – no proprietary connector to build against. Local iteration: DuckHog, a DuckDB extension that lets local compute pull subsets of warehouse data into pandas, polars, or DuckDB itself, iterate quickly, and write results back. For an agent that wants fast local loops instead of round-tripping every query to the cluster, this is the better pattern. Agents read your data and drive development None of this matters to an agent unless the agent can actually query it. PostHog exposes the context warehouse over MCP , PostHog Web , Slack , or PostHog Code . An agent working the self-driving product loop reads product events and business context through the identical interface a human would use in the SQL editor. That's what makes this a context warehouse rather than a data warehouse with an AI feature bolted on: the context an agent needs to make a good decision is already there, and it can use it to drive development autonomously or answer your questions. What's in the pipeline The context warehouse today is deliberately not a full data stack: land your events and your business data in one place, let the tools you already use in PostHog query it directly to make better decisions about the direction of your product. Here's what we're already building toward: Direction What it means Making our Managed Warehouse generally available Right now, we're in a closed beta that will be open very soon, you can get on the waitlist and be the first to hear about it. Deeper modeling Closing the gap with dbt-style transformation maturity for teams with more advanced modeling needs. More sources Expanding Warehouse Sources coverage so fewer teams need a custom sync to get their systems in. More of the loop exposed to agents As the self-driving product loop matures, more of what an agent can see in the context warehouse becomes something it can act on directly, not just read. Try it yourself Join the waitlist for the managed warehouse beta, or just connect your first source and get a head start, no need to wait around for us. Once you're in, the warehouse lives inside PostHog, same as everything else: sync a source through Warehouse Sources, poke at it in the SQL editor, or hand an agent the keys and see what it does with it. FAQ Is a context warehouse the same as a data lakehouse? No. A lakehouse combines warehouse and data-lake storage patterns. A context warehouse adds the ability for your product tools and agents to query that storage natively, without a separate BI or reverse-ETL layer. Can I use a context warehouse if I already have a data warehouse? Yes. Sync your data into PostHog via Warehouse Sources, and that data becomes queryable alongside your product events in analytics, experiments, and agents. No migration required. Does a context warehouse replace Fivetran, dbt, and Looker? For most product teams, yes. Ingestion (Warehouse Sources), modeling, and querying are built in. Teams with advanced modeling needs may still want dedicated tooling for now. What's the difference between a context warehouse and a CDP? A CDP moves customer data between tools. The context warehouse is the storage and query layer those tools run on top of, which can include a CDP. Is my data still mine, can I export it? Yes. It's stored in S3 in your organization's partition, accessible over a standard Postgres wire protocol connection, not locked behind a proprietary format. PostHog is the leading platform for building self-driving products. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability , product analytics , session replay , feature flags , experiments , error tracking , logs , and more – PostHog captures all the context agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack , the web app , the desktop ( PostHog Desktop ), or your own editor via the MCP . Community questions

title: CrowdStrike Expands Project QuiltWorks with AWS, Hardening the Cloud Attack Surface Against Frontier AI Risk

body_text: CrowdStrike unites the cloud infrastructure layer with the intelligence of the only coalition spanning discovery, prioritization, remediation, and financial protection to harden against frontier AI vulnerabilities AUSTIN, Texas and NEW YORK – AWS Summit New York – June 17, 2026 – CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD) today announced that it is expanding Project QuiltWorks with Amazon Web Services (AWS), extending the coalition from the technology, services, and financial protection to mitigate frontier AI risk, to the attack surface where vulnerabilities live and are exploited. As frontier AI collapses the window between vulnerability and exploitation – marking a significant inflection point in cybersecurity history – QuiltWorks has systematically united every layer of the response. With over 110 native AWS integrations, CrowdStrike is helping organizations running workloads on AWS gain continuous visibility into vulnerabilities and prioritize remediation across the enterprise regardless of where their applications and data reside. With the addition of AWS, the coalition now includes workload infrastructure, hardening against frontier AI vulnerabilities and providing a path to address the critical needs of large production workloads that enterprises run in the cloud. title: Vacation-Proof Your Home Before You Leave
summary: Mercury Insurance shares 10 simple steps to help homeowners avoid costly surprises while they're away LOS ANGELES, July 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mercury Insurance (NYSE/NYSE TX: MCY) is encouraging...
body_text: Mercury Insurance shares 10 simple steps to help homeowners avoid costly surprises while they're away LOS ANGELES , July 9, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- Mercury Insurance (NYSE/NYSE TX: MCY) is encouraging homeowners to take a few simple precautions before leaving for vacation as new research shows nearly two-thirds of summer travelers admit they could do a better job protecting their homes while they're away. Whether you're heading out for a long weekend or an extended getaway, spending a few extra minutes preparing your home can help reduce the risk of theft, water damage, electrical issues and other costly surprises. "Preparing your home before a vacation doesn't have to take hours, but it can make a meaningful difference," said Larry Anderson, Director of Underwriting Operations for Mercury Insurance. "Simple habits like checking your water supply, making your home appear occupied and asking someone you trust to keep an eye on the property can help homeowners return home with greater peace of mind." Many of the most common vacation-related home losses are preventable. Mercury recommends homeowners add these 10 steps to every pre-vacation checklist: 1. Lock every door and window Double-check all entry points before leaving, including garage doors, side gates and second-story windows that may have been left open. Don't forget to secure sliding glass doors and any detached structures, such as sheds. 2. Make your home look lived in Use timers or smart-home automation to turn lights on and off at different times. If possible, vary lighting schedules in different rooms. A home that appears occupied is generally less attractive to potential burglars. 3. Pause mail and package deliveries Overflowing mail, newspapers and packages can quickly signal that no one is home. Consider placing a temporary hold on deliveries or asking a trusted neighbor to collect them while you're away. 4. Consider shutting off your home's main water supply Water damage can become significantly more expensive when a leak goes unnoticed for days. If practical, shutting off the main water supply before an extended trip can help prevent a minor plumbing issue from becoming a major repair. 5. Adjust your thermostat Set your thermostat to maintain a safe indoor temperature while reducing unnecessary energy use. Smart thermostats also allow homeowners to monitor conditions and make adjustments remotely if weather changes unexpectedly. 6. Test smoke alarms and smart home devices Before leaving, test smoke alarms, carbon monoxide detectors and any smart leak or security sensors. Replace batteries if needed and confirm your monitoring apps are functioning properly. 7. Ask someone you trust to check on your home A friend, family member or neighbor can spot problems before they become major losses. Periodic visits can help identify storm damage, irrigation issues, fallen tree limbs or signs of forced entry. 8. Save vacation photos for after you return Sharing travel updates in real time may unintentionally advertise that your home is vacant. Waiting until you're home helps protect both your privacy and your property. 9. Tidy up your yard Mow the lawn, trim overgrown landscaping and put away outdoor equipment before leaving. A well-maintained property gives the appearance that someone is home and paying attention. 10. Review your homeowners insurance Before your trip, take a few minutes to review your homeowners policy, verify your contact information and know how to reach your insurance company if something happens while you're away. "A vacation should end with great memories, not an unexpected repair bill," Anderson said. "Taking a few simple steps before you leave can help protect your home, reduce unnecessary stress and give you greater peace of mind while you're away." For more information about homeowners insurance coverage and ways to help protect your home year-round, visit the Mercury Insurance Resource Center . About Mercury Insurance Mercury Insurance (NYSE: MCY) is a multiple-line insurance carrier predominantly offering personal auto, homeowners, renters and commercial insurance through a network of independent agents in Arizona, California, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oklahoma, Texas and Virginia, as well as auto insurance in Florida. Mercury writes other lines of insurance in various states, including commercial, business owners and business auto, landlord, home-sharing, ride-hailing and mechanical protection insurance. Since 1962, Mercury has provided customers with tremendous value for their insurance dollar by pairing ultra-competitive rates with excellent customer service, through more than 4,200 employees and a network of more than 6,340 independent agents in 11 states. Mercury has earned an "A" rating from A.M. Best, as well as "Best Auto Insurance Company" designations from Forbes and Insure.com. For more information visit www.MercuryInsurance.com or follow the company on LinkedIn , Instagram or Facebook . Media interested in receiving updates from Mercury can learn more at the Mercury Newsroom . SOURCE Mercury Insurance

title: HII Hosts Australian Minister for Defence Industry at Newport News Shipbuilding Charleston Operations
summary: HII is America's largest military shipbuilding company, delivering advanced warships, submarines, and mission technology solutions in service of the nation.
body_text: Photo caption: HII hosted Australian Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy at the company’s Newport News Shipbuilding Charleston Operations site in Goose Creek, South Carolina on Monday, July 27, 2026 (Photo by Todd Corillo/HII). GOOSE CREEK, S.C., July 27, 2026 — HII (NYSE: HII) hosted Australian Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy today at the company’s Newport News Shipbuilding Charleston Operations site in South Carolina. The visit was held in support of the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom and United States (AUKUS) partnership. HII continues its commitment to supporting AUKUS and the optimal pathway for Australia’s acquisition of a conventionally armed, nuclear-powered, submarine capability and a broader partnership on advanced capabilities. The visit included a tour of the production facility and discussions with company leaders about HII’s distributed shipbuilding initiative to increase shipbuilding throughput and meet the increased demand for ships. Under HII’s ownership, the site has increased production by more than 50% as it continues to ramp up in support of U.S. Navy programs. “It was a pleasure to tour this facility and see firsthand the capability established here, and the impact it is already having on the U.S. submarine industrial base,” Conroy said. “I look forward to seeing Australian-made parts coming through this, and other U.S. facilities, demonstrating the strength of the AUKUS partnership and our shared commitment to industrial uplift.” NNS Charleston Operations is located on 45 acres along the Cooper River with more than 480,000 square feet of covered manufacturing space. It is strategically located within South Carolina’s rapidly growing maritime ecosystem, having both barge and rail access, capacity to expand, and growing access to the highly skilled maritime trades workforce. “We are honored Minister Conroy chose to invest time with us at HII during his trip to the United States,” said Matt Needy, NNS vice president of Charleston Operations. “We value the opportunity to share best practices from our expanded operations, here in South Carolina, to help accelerate AUKUS momentum.” HII is actively supporting a range of initiatives to advance the AUKUS trilateral security partnership. HII was awarded the contract to deliver the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification (AUSSQ) Program, which accelerates the identification, development and qualification of Australian suppliers for integration into the United States submarine industrial base. HII is also working with Australian industry and academia to develop the skilled workforce needed to support Australia’s nuclear-powered submarine enterprise. This includes educating and training thousands of engineers, maritime specialists, nuclear tradespeople and other professionals to support the enterprise across its full lifecycle. A cornerstone initiative under AUKUS Pillar I, AUSSQ is strengthening Australia’s sovereign nuclear-powered submarine capability by qualifying Australian small and medium-sized enterprises to participate in the U.S. and U.K. nuclear submarine supply chains. The program spans seven critical work packages supporting the construction and sustainment of Virginia -class submarines and the future SSN-AUKUS platform. To date, AUSSQ has qualified 13 Australian suppliers, providing them with a pathway into U.S. and U.K. nuclear submarine programs and embedding Australian industry into AUKUS submarine production and sustainment.
